title: The Fox Who Was Taken In
intro: A fox overhears some villagers using his name for a trickster. Delighted with his fame, he imagines the festivities they might hold if he paid a visit in person. Shawqi gives him ample time to picture his reception and very little time to enjoy the real one. Osama Al-Waaedh repeats the closing couplet.

translation: The fox heard the village folk
call out to a swindler, “You fox.”
1.sharh: An animal has the uncanny experience of overhearing its name used figuratively. The villagers mean a human swindler, and the fox is free to misjudge what they think of either of them.

translation: “Here indeed,” he said, “is the height of fame,
a thing no one can give or go and seek.
2.sharh: He takes the unbidden mention of his name as the highest sort of fame, beyond patronage or deliberate pursuit. He has yet to consider the company his name is keeping.

translation: Who has wits to match mine, when humankind
3.sharh: To be made a proverb is to pass into ordinary speech as an example. The fox cites his failure to understand such a saying as evidence of his exceptional wit.

translation: What harm in paying them a visit
and showing them more than they marvelled at?
4.sharh: His reasoning has carried him from a figure of speech to a personal appearance. What he supposes the villagers will admire is also what they have learned to guard against.

translation: Perhaps they’ll hold a fête for me,
with the cock or the rabbit there.”
5.sharh: The guest list has been chosen with a fox’s appetite. Even his fantasy of being honoured includes the prospect of a meal.

translation: He made for the villagers and greeted them,
then took his stand among them for a speech.
6.sharh: The visitor supplies the greeting and the speech himself. The villagers have so far had no reason to depart from their original, unflattering opinion.

translation: They took their visitor by the ear
and gave him to the dog to play with.
7.sharh: The Arabic suddenly uses two passives. The creature who arranged the entire fête in his head is now an object to be picked up and passed along.

translation: Never put your trust in a master of tricks.
Even a fox sometimes gets taken in.
8.sharh: Cunning turns out to be an unreliable guarantee even for its owner. The creature whose name means a deceiver has managed, with very little help, to deceive himself.

1.2.2.head: مُحتال
1.2.2.meaning: A trickster or swindler, the person actually being addressed.

1.2.3-4.head: يا ثَعلَب
1.2.3-4.meaning: “You fox”, a direct quotation used as a name for the trickster.

2.1.4.head: غايَة
2.1.4.meaning: The furthest limit or pinnacle of something.

2.2.2.head: الفَخر
2.2.2.meaning: Grounds for pride, which the fox believes the villagers have given him.

2.2.4.head: آتى
2.2.4.meaning: Bestowed. In the passive, nobody can grant such fame as a favour.

3.1.3.meaning: Wits or understanding, the faculty that checks foolish impulses.

3.1.6.meaning: Humankind, the people among whom the saying circulates.

3.2.3-4.head: مَثَل يُضرَب
3.2.3-4.meaning: “A proverb that is struck”, an example invoked whenever a similar case arises.

4.1.4.head: وافى
4.1.4.meaning: Came in person, arrived for a visit.

4.2.4.head: اِستَغرَبَ
4.2.4.meaning: Found something remarkable. The fox takes their interest for admiration.

5.1.4.head: زينَة
5.1.4.meaning: A festive occasion with public display or decoration.

5.2.2.head: الدّيك
5.2.2.meaning: The cock is the subject of “attend”. One printing gives the accusative ending where the construction calls for the nominative.

6.2.4.head: خَطَبَ
6.2.4.meaning: Addressed a gathering as a formal speaker.

7.1.2.head: الزّائِر
7.1.2.meaning: The visitor, still described in the language of hospitality as he is seized.

7.2.1.head: أَعطى
7.2.1.meaning: Handed over, the moment the guest passes from the villagers into the dog’s power.

8.1.4-5.head: ذو حيلَة
8.1.4-5.meaning: Someone skilled in stratagems and in finding a way out.

8.2.3.head: اِنخَدَعَ
8.2.3.meaning: Was taken in, the answering form of the verb “to deceive”.
